newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs seen benefitting from mortgage firm scheme.
newsitem.headline: JGBs seen benefitting from mortgage firm scheme.

text.p: Japanese Government Bonds (JGBs) are likely to be among the beneficiaries of massive funds arising from a government scheme to solve the financial problems of failed mortgage companies, traders said on Tuesday.

However, they said the flow of cash into JGBs may not be hefty enough to justify the recent bond market rally, which has been based on speculation that most of the money will eventually be poured into JGBs.
Some 5.4 trillion yen of new cash arising from the scheme is available, in theory, for capital market investment, traders said.
On Thursday, the Housing Loan Administration Corp, the body set up to collect problem loans incurred by failed mortgage firms, said it had started investing the funds it inherited from the firms.
Traders estimated that the body has parked about one trillion yen in money market instruments such as certificates of deposit (CDs) and commercial paper.

The loan-collecting body inherited assets and debts of housing loan companies on October 1. An unusually large amount of CDs was issued last week in response to the Corporation's buying interest, traders said.

Approximately 907 billion yen of cash will be disbursed by banks to the "Financial Stabilisation Fund" set up at the government's Deposit Insurance Corp in July as part of a government scheme to wind up failed mortgage firms.
Traders said there was a rumour the Fund would buy 20-year JGBs offered on Tuesday, as its portfolio has a 15-year maturity.
The government has another fund worth 800 billion, excluding a 100 billion contribution from the Bank of Japan (BOJ), under the wind-up scheme.

The largest part of the money that will become available under the scheme is the 2.7 trillion yen the nation's agricultural financial institutions are expected to receive, possibly in late November, traders said. The agricultural financial sector was obliged to pay 530 billion yen to the scheme, however, it will recover the remaining 2.7 trillion yen in loans it previously made to the mortgage firms.

Masayoshi Hasegawa, assistant manager of Norinchukin Bank's capital markets division, said: "It may be too optimistic if the market expects half of the 2.7 trillion to be smoothly funnelled into bonds."
Norinchukin is a huge bank which is Japan's central agricultural financial institution.

Hasegawa said the only explanation for the recent bond market rally, and the resulting extremely low yields, would be that it was fuelled by intensive speculation that the JGB market would be the main beneficiary of the massive funds.

"However, it might be too early to count on those funds as financial institutions already have their own annual portfolio plans, and a temporary fund surplus, if any, is unlikely to have a decisive impact on their strategy," Hasegawa said.

On Monday, in response to dealers' speculative purchases, the key December JGB contract hit an all-time high of 123.45 and the benchmark 10-year cash bond yield fell to a 10-month low of 2.710 percent. The December was about 123.20 on Tuesday.
Some bond strategists see a chance of some cooling of the speculation that money will keep coming into bonds.

Neale Vincent, bond strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities (Japan), said: "Although there are plenty of reasons to buy JGBs, I expect some correction beginning sometime in the next few weeks because we have not had any break since July." -- Tokyo Treasury Desk, 813-3432-8676
